findings.title: Empty email error arrays disable signup after unrelated validation failures
findings.description:
The condition treats `result.errors.email` as evidence of an email error, but an empty JavaScript array is truthy. The new validator reads `record.errors[attribute]` even for valid emails (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13`). In the supported Rails 3.2 errors implementation, this initializes an empty error array that is retained by `user.errors.to_hash`.

Consequently, a signup rejected only for another field, such as a short password, can return `email: []`. This code then caches the valid email as rejected, disabling submission even after the other field is corrected.

Require a nonempty email error array before rejecting the address. Add a regression test showing that a non-email validation failure leaves the same email usable.

findings.title: Domain casing bypasses blocked-email matching
findings.description:
Blocked addresses are matched using exact string equality, without normalizing either stored addresses or lookup values. `User.new_from_params` assigns the supplied email unchanged, so a block for `block@spamfromhome.org` does not match `block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG`, although both identify the same mailbox.

Normalize at least the domain consistently when storing and checking blocked addresses, following the existing `Email.downcase` convention. Ensure existing rows are handled, and add tests for mixed-case domains.

findings.title: Concurrent matches lose counter increments
findings.description:
The read-modify-save sequence is not atomic. Two concurrent checks can read the same `match_count`, increment it locally, and both save the same resulting value, recording only one match.

Use an atomic database increment, with the timestamp update handled consistently, and add coverage for concurrent updates.
